sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Founders are developers who do not call it that
sections.para: Every GenAI founder Dinis knows does a development team's jobs and denies being a developer, because they never saw how rough new technology is inside. Since a book addressed to a word its readers reject loses them, his hypothesis is to call it Generation ZX Founders, with the reveal at the end.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Developers in all but name; rename the book
sections.para: Founders do the roles of a whole team, often no worse than the industry. They only saw polished products, and now meet the non-functional requirements. Programming was never just code. So the book may be Generation ZX Founders.

sections.label: The look they give me
sections.line: They laugh when told they are developers
sections.para: Friends building companies deny being developers: they just tell the model what to do. Yet they write requirements, test, release and direct a team of agents, mostly in the explorer phase, some assembling commodity components.

sections.label: Crude, compared to what?
sections.line: Crude, but the industry often does worse
sections.para: Many companies underinvest, outsource, underfund teams and ship anyway, which is why vulnerabilities are everywhere, even in big companies' internal tools. A vulnerability is an engineering gap; internal tools never had the market's beating, which is where the SaaS apocalypse may land first.

sections.label: They never saw the sausage factory
sections.line: They never saw how new products really work
sections.para: Founders know polished, later-generation products. The iPhone was launched on a golden path of taps with signal bars hard-coded; Windows 98 crashed on stage beside Gates; Apple's interfaces began as Director mock-ups. The demo gods are explorer technology hanging by a thread.

sections.label: The pilot who is relieved to land
sections.line: The demo team's relief worries the customer
sections.para: When a demo works, the presenters are visibly relieved, and the customer wonders whether it was supposed to fail, like a pilot celebrating a safe landing.

sections.label: Make it look unfinished
sections.line: Unfinished work made to look unfinished
sections.para: Developers gave mock-ups rough, hand-drawn themes so the business would not ship them, as Bootswatch's Sketchy and Napkin Look and Feel do, following Joel Spolsky's 2002 point that a beautiful screen looks almost done to a non-programmer.

sections.label: Now they understand
sections.line: Now they meet the non-functional requirements
sections.para: Building for themselves, business people now complain about versioning, breakage, design alignment, stability and security, the requirements that were never funded. Seeing inside a technology company would show them how good they already are.

sections.label: Programming is not writing code
sections.line: Programming is not just writing code
sections.para: People who say they do not program build serious things in Excel and professional tools. That is programming; code is a small part of development, and the citizen developer is good news.

sections.label: Call the book what they are
sections.para: Calling readers developers loses the people the book is for; founder is a word they recognise. Decision 019 adopted Generation ZX Founders (GenAI Edition) the same day, keeping 'you are a developer' as the turn of the book in the frame chapter rather than a last-page reveal.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Experience, sources, and a title since adopted
sections.para: Every founder Dinis knows is his experience. The title was a hypothesis, adopted by decision 019 the same day. The iPhone story is one reporter's account; Apple's Director prototypes were internal. Being a developer does not mean the work is ready.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: A memo and the primary sources
sections.para: Dinis's memo of 19 October 2026, Vogelstein's NYT Magazine piece, the 1998 AP report, James Thomson on the Dock, Joel Spolsky, Bootswatch and Napkin, and the book's decisions.
